blocks.x: Introduction
With $k$ regressors $x_1,\dots,x_k$,
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\dots+\beta_kx_k+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\Normal(0,\sigma^2).

The model is linear because it is linear in the parameters $\beta_j$; the regressors themselves may be nonlinear functions (squares, products, logarithms). The coefficient $\beta_j$ is the change in the mean response per unit change in $x_j$ with the other regressors held fixed.

Models that look more complicated are still multiple linear regression models. A cubic in one regressor, $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3+\varepsilon$, becomes linear on setting $x_1=x$, $x_2=x^2$, $x_3=x^3$. An interaction $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_{12}x_1x_2+\varepsilon$ is linear with $x_3=x_1x_2$, $\beta_3=\beta_{12}$. The second-order model with interaction, $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_{11}x_1^2+\beta_{22}x_2^2+\beta_{12}x_1x_2+\varepsilon$, is likewise linear with five regressors; its surface can be a mound, a saddle or a ridge depending on the coefficients. Any model linear in the $\beta$’s is a linear regression model, regardless of the shape of the surface it generates. Interaction means that the effect of changing $x_1$ depends on the level of $x_2$: in the model with $\beta_{12}$, $\partial\,\Exp(Y)/\partial x_1=\beta_1+\beta_{12}x_2$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Textbook example: wire bond pull strength

blocks.x: For $25$ wire bonds, regress pull strength $y$ on wire length $x_1$ and die height $x_2$. The normal equations (with the sums from the data table) are

with solution $\hat\beta_0=2.26379$, $\hat\beta_1=2.74427$, $\hat\beta_2=0.01253$. The matrix route $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$ gives the same values. The estimated error variance is $\hat\sigma^2=5.2364$ and the standard errors are $\se(\hat\beta_0)=1.060$, $\se(\hat\beta_1)=0.09352$, $\se(\hat\beta_2)=0.002798$ (precisely estimated slopes; the intercept is relatively less precise).
Eight observations on a response $y$ with two coded regressors $x_1,x_2\in\{-1,+1\}$:
Least Squares Estimation of the Parameters
Given $n$ observations $(y_i,x_{i1},\dots,x_{ik})$, the least squares estimates minimise
L=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(y_i-\beta_0-\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jx_{ij}\Big)^2.
Setting each partial derivative to zero gives $p=k+1$ normal equations in the $p$ unknowns. In matrix form they are very compact.
Matrix Approach to Multiple Linear Regression
Write

\mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}y_1\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix},\quad X=\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{11}&\cdots&x_{1k}\\\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&\cdots&x_{nk}\end{pmatrix},\quad\boldsymbol\beta=\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\vdots\\\beta_k\end{pmatrix},\quad\boldsymbol\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_1\\\vdots\\\varepsilon_n\end{pmatrix},
so that $\mathbf{y}=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, with $X$ the $n\times p$ design matrix.
If $X\T X$ is invertible (the columns of $X$ are linearly independent),
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y},

the unique solution of the normal equations $X\T X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=X\T\mathbf{y}$. The fitted values are $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=H\mathbf{y}$ with the hat matrix $H=X(X\T X)^{-1}X\T$, and the residuals are $\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}=(I-H)\mathbf{y}$.

$L=(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)\T(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)$ has gradient $-2X\T(\mathbf{y}-X\boldsymbol\beta)$, which vanishes at the stated $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, and the Hessian $2X\T X$ is positive definite, so this is the unique minimum.

$H$ is symmetric and idempotent ($H^2=H$) with $\tr H=p$; it is the orthogonal projection of $\R^n$ onto the column space of $X$. Consequently $X\T\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{0}$: the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of $X$, and with an intercept column, $\sum e_i=0$.
$SS_E=\mathbf{e}\T\mathbf{e}=\mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{y}-\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\T X\T\mathbf{y}$ and $\hat\sigma^2=MS_E=\dfrac{SS_E}{n-p}$, with $p=k+1$ parameters.

Here $X\T X=\diag(8,8,8)$, since the columns $\mathbf{1}$, $x_1$, $x_2$ are mutually orthogonal, so $(X\T X)^{-1}=\tfrac18I$ and each coefficient is a simple average: $\hat\beta_0=\bar{y}=17.1$, $\hat\beta_1=\tfrac18\sum x_{i1}y_i=24.0/8=3.0$, $\hat\beta_2=\tfrac18\sum x_{i2}y_i=12.4/8=1.55$. The fitted equation is $\hat{y}=17.1+3.0x_1+1.55x_2$. The fitted values are $12.55,\,12.55,\,15.65,\,15.65,\,18.55,\,18.55,\,21.65,\,21.65$, the residuals are $-0.45,\,0.45,\,-0.45,\,0.45,\,-0.65,\,0.65,\,-0.65,\,0.65$, $SS_E=4(0.2025)+4(0.4225)=2.5$ and $\hat\sigma^2=2.5/(8-3)=0.5$.
Properties of the Least Squares Estimators
Under the model with $\Exp[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\mathbf{0}$ and $\Cov[\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\sigma^2I$:

$\Exp[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$; write $C_{jj}$ for the $j$-th diagonal entry of $(X\T X)^{-1}$, so $\Var[\hat\beta_j]=\sigma^2C_{jj}$ and $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$;
$\Exp[\hat\sigma^2]=\sigma^2$;
(Gauss–Markov) among all linear unbiased estimators, $\hat\beta_j$ has minimum variance;

if $\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\Normal(\mathbf{0},\sigma^2I)$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\sim\Normal\big(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}\big)$, $\ (n-p)\hat\sigma^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_{n-p}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is independent of $\hat\sigma^2$.

(i) $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T(X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=\boldsymbol\beta+(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, so $\Exp[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\,\sigma^2I\,X(X\T X)^{-1}=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$. (ii) $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ because $(I-H)X=0$; then $\Exp(\mathbf{e}\T\mathbf{e})=\Exp[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\T(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon]=\sigma^2\tr(I-H)=\sigma^2(n-p)$. (iv) $(I-H)$ is the projection onto a subspace of dimension $n-p$, so with orthonormal coordinates adapted to that subspace $\boldsymbol\varepsilon\T(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon/\sigma^2$ is a sum of $n-p$ squared independent standard normals; independence of $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ follows because $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ and $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ are jointly normal and uncorrelated ($X\T(I-H)=0$). (iii) Any other linear unbiased estimator $A\mathbf{y}$ has $AX=I$; write $A=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T+D$ with $DX=0$, so $\Cov(A\mathbf{y})=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}+\sigma^2DD\T\succeq\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$.

In the running example $C_{jj}=1/8$ for each coefficient, so $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{0.5/8}=0.25$ for $j=0,1,2$, and $\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2$ are uncorrelated (the off-diagonal entries of $(X\T X)^{-1}$ are $0$). The hat matrix diagonal is $h_{ii}=\tfrac38$ for every observation, which sums to $p=3$.

sections.title: Hypothesis Tests in Multiple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Test for Significance of Regression
$SS_T=\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2=\mathbf{y}\T\mathbf{y}-n\bar{y}^2$, $\ SS_R=\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\T X\T\mathbf{y}-n\bar{y}^2$ and $SS_E=SS_T-SS_R$, with degrees of freedom $n-1=k+(n-p)$.
To test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\dots=\beta_k=0$ against $H_1:$ at least one $\beta_j\ne0$, use
F_0=\frac{SS_R/k}{SS_E/(n-p)}=\frac{MS_R}{MS_E}\sim F_{k,\,n-p}\ \text{ under }H_0.
Reject $H_0$ if $f_0>f_{\alpha,k,n-p}$.
$R^2=SS_R/SS_T$ and
R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=1-\frac{SS_E/(n-p)}{SS_T/(n-1)}.
$R^2$ never decreases when a regressor is added; $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$ penalises extra regressors (it can decrease) and is preferred for comparing models of different size.
Tests on Individual Regression Coefficients and Subsets of Coefficients

To test $H_0:\beta_j=0$ against $H_1:\beta_j\ne0$ use $T_0=\hat\beta_j/\se(\hat\beta_j)\sim t_{n-p}$ under $H_0$, and reject if $\abs{t_0}>t_{\alpha/2,n-p}$. For the one-sided alternatives, reject $H_1:\beta_j>0$ if $t_0>t_{\alpha,n-p}$ and $H_1:\beta_j<0$ if $t_0<-t_{\alpha,n-p}$. This is a marginal test: it asks whether $x_j$ adds anything given that all the other regressors are already in the model.
$t_0=3.0/0.25=12.0$ for $\beta_1$ and $1.55/0.25=6.2$ for $\beta_2$, both exceeding $t_{0.025,5}=2.571$: both regressors are significant.

A subset of coefficients is tested by the extra sum of squares method. Partition $\boldsymbol\beta=(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2)$, with $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ containing $r$ coefficients, and test $H_0:\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf{0}$ against $H_1:\boldsymbol\beta_2\ne\mathbf{0}$. Fit the full model and the reduced model (without $\boldsymbol\beta_2$); the improvement in the regression sum of squares is
SS_R(\boldsymbol\beta_2\mid\boldsymbol\beta_1)=SS_R(\text{full})-SS_R(\text{reduced})=SS_E(\text{reduced})-SS_E(\text{full}).
Under $H_0:\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf{0}$,
F_0=\frac{SS_R(\boldsymbol\beta_2\mid\boldsymbol\beta_1)/r}{MS_E(\text{full})}\sim F_{r,\,n-p},
and $H_0$ is rejected if $f_0>f_{\alpha,r,n-p}$. When $r=1$, $F_0=T_0^2$ for the $t$-test of that coefficient.

Test whether $x_2$ adds anything to a model already containing $x_1$: the reduced model $\hat{y}=17.1+3.0x_1$ has $SS_R=72$, so $SS_R(\beta_2\mid\beta_1)=91.22-72=19.22$, and $F_0=19.22/0.5=38.4=6.2^2$ (compare $f_{0.05,1,5}=6.61$): significant.

For the wire bond fit ($n=25$, $p=3$, so $22$ error degrees of freedom): $SS_T=6105.9447$, $SS_R=5990.7712$, $SS_E=115.1735$. Then $f_0\approx572\gg f_{0.05,2,22}=3.44$, so the regression is significant: pull strength is linearly related to wire length, die height, or both. This does not by itself show the model is adequate for prediction, which needs the checks of Section 6.5. $R^2=5990.7712/6105.9447=0.9811$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.979$, against $R^2=0.9640$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.962$ for the one-variable model with wire length alone: adding die height raises $R^2$ by only $0.0171$ but also raises $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$, so it is a genuine improvement. For $H_0:\beta_2=0$: $t_0=4.4767>t_{0.025,22}=2.074$ ($P=0.0002$), so die height contributes given wire length. The partial $F$-statistic is $t_0^2\approx20.0>f_{0.05,1,22}=4.30$, the same conclusion.
More About the Extra Sum of Squares Method (CD Only)

With an orthogonal design (as above), $SS_R(\beta_2\mid\beta_1)=SS_R(\beta_2)$: the contribution of each regressor does not depend on the order in which they are entered. In non-orthogonal data it does, and the contributions generally do not add to $SS_R$. The sequential (“Type I”) sums of squares depend on the order of entry, the partial (“Type III”) sums of squares measure each regressor’s contribution given all the others and are equivalent to the $t$-tests. The extra sum of squares framework also tests any linear restriction $C\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf{0}$ via $F_0=\dfrac{(SS_E(\text{restricted})-SS_E(\text{full}))/r}{MS_E(\text{full})}$.

sections.title: Confidence Intervals in Multiple Linear Regression

blocks.x: Confidence Intervals on Individual Regression Coefficients

$\hat\beta_j-t_{\alpha/2,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}\le\beta_j\le\hat\beta_j+t_{\alpha/2,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$ (two-sided, $\alpha/2$ in each tail). One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds use $t_{\alpha,n-p}$ and one limit: $\beta_j\le\hat\beta_j+t_{\alpha,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$ (upper) or $\hat\beta_j-t_{\alpha,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}\le\beta_j$ (lower). Likewise for the mean-response and prediction intervals below: replace $t_{\alpha/2,n-p}$ by $t_{\alpha,n-p}$ and keep one limit.
Confidence Interval on the Mean Response

At a point $\mathbf{x}_0=(1,x_{01},\dots,x_{0k})\T$ the mean response is $\mu_{Y|\mathbf{x}_0}=\mathbf{x}_0\T\boldsymbol\beta$, estimated by $\hat\mu=\mathbf{x}_0\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ with $\Var[\hat\mu]=\sigma^2\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0$.
$\hat\mu_{Y|\mathbf{x}_0}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\,\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0}$.

At $\mathbf{x}_0=(1,1,1)\T$: $\hat\mu=17.1+3.0+1.55=21.65$ and $\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0=3/8$, so the standard error is $\sqrt{0.5\cdot3/8}=0.433$ and the $95\%$ interval is $21.65\pm2.571(0.433)=21.65\pm1.11$.

The prediction interval is always wider than the confidence interval on the mean response at the same point, because it adds the inherent variability of a single new $Y$ to the error of estimating the mean.
A $100(1-\alpha)\%$ prediction interval for a new observation at $\mathbf{x}_0$ is $\hat{y}_0\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-p}\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\big(1+\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0\big)}$.

In several dimensions a point can lie inside the range of each regressor separately yet far from the cloud of data jointly (a hidden extrapolation). The quantity $h_{00}=\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0$ detects this: if it exceeds $\max_ih_{ii}$ the point lies outside the regressor variable hull and predictions there are unreliable.
Residual Analysis

The residuals $\mathbf{e}=(I-H)\mathbf{y}$ have $\Cov(\mathbf{e})=\sigma^2(I-H)$, so $\Var[e_i]=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})$: residuals at high-leverage points are artificially small. Several scalings are used.

Standardised residual $d_i=e_i/\hat\sigma$; studentised residual $r_i=\dfrac{e_i}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})}}$, which has approximately unit variance for every observation. Values with $\abs{r_i}>3$ are potential outliers.

The plots of Chapter 5 apply: normal probability plot of the residuals, residuals versus $\hat{y}_i$, residuals versus each regressor $x_j$ (curvature suggests a missing quadratic term) and residuals versus time order. The prediction residual $e_{(i)}=e_i/(1-h_{ii})$ is the error when observation $i$ is left out of the fit, and $PRESS=\sum e_{(i)}^2$ measures predictive ability.
Influential Observations

The leverage of observation $i$ is $h_{ii}=\mathbf{x}_i\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i$, the weight that $y_i$ has on its own fitted value ($\hat{y}_i=\sum_jh_{ij}y_j$); $0\le h_{ii}\le1$ and $\sum h_{ii}=p$, so the average leverage is $p/n$. Observations with $h_{ii}>2p/n$ have high leverage. Cook’s distance
D_i=\frac{r_i^2}p\cdot\frac{h_{ii}}{1-h_{ii}}
measures how much all fitted values change when observation $i$ is deleted; $D_i>1$ marks an influential point.

An observation is influential when it combines high leverage (unusual $x$) with a large residual; a high-leverage point lying exactly on the trend merely sharpens the fit, while an outlier at a low-leverage point shifts the line little. Investigate (do not automatically delete) influential points.
Polynomial Regression Models

A curved relationship can be fitted by including powers of a regressor: $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\varepsilon$ (quadratic) is a linear model in $(x,x^2)$, so all of the above applies with $x_1=x$, $x_2=x^2$. Guidelines: keep the order low (degree $\le2$ or $3$); retain lower-order terms when a higher-order term is included; centre $x$ (use $x-\bar{x}$) to reduce the strong correlation between $x$ and $x^2$ that makes $X\T X$ ill-conditioned; and extrapolate with great caution since polynomials behave wildly outside the data range. Interaction terms $x_1x_2$ let the effect of $x_1$ depend on the level of $x_2$.
Categorical Regressors and Indicator Variables

A qualitative factor with $m$ levels is represented by $m-1$ indicator (dummy) variables. For a two-level factor (e.g. machine A or B) let $x=0$ for A and $x=1$ for B. In $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x+\varepsilon$, the coefficient $\beta_2$ is the difference between B and A at a fixed $x_1$: machine A has intercept $\beta_0$ and machine B intercept $\beta_0+\beta_2$, with parallel lines. Adding the product $x_1x$ allows different slopes. With $m=3$ levels use two indicators; using $m$ indicators together with an intercept makes $X\T X$ singular (the dummy-variable trap).
Selection of Variables and Model Building

With many candidate regressors we want a model that is simple yet predicts well. Adding regressors always reduces $SS_E$ but inflates the variance of predictions and risks fitting noise (overfitting).

All possible regressions for $k$ candidates ($2^k$ models) compared by $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$, $MS_E$, the PRESS statistic, Mallows’ $C_p=\dfrac{SS_E(p)}{\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{full}}}-n+2p$ (a good model has $C_p\approx p$) or AIC$=n\ln(SS_E/n)+2p$.

Stepwise methods use partial $F$-statistics with an entry threshold $f_{\mathrm{in}}$ and a removal threshold $f_{\mathrm{out}}$, $f_{\mathrm{in}}\ge f_{\mathrm{out}}$ (software often uses $\alpha=0.15$ to enter and remove, $0.10$ for backward elimination). Stepwise regression starts with the regressor most highly correlated with $y$ (largest $F$), then at each step adds the candidate with the largest partial $F$ if it exceeds $f_{\mathrm{in}}$, and afterwards deletes any included regressor whose partial $F$ falls below $f_{\mathrm{out}}$; it stops when nothing can be added or removed. Forward selection only adds, never testing earlier entries for removal, which is its weakness. Backward elimination starts with all $K$ candidates and repeatedly removes the one with the smallest partial $F$ if it is below $f_{\mathrm{out}}$. Because the variable chosen is the one that maximises $F$, the advertised significance level is not the true level, and the degrees of freedom of $MS_E$ change from step to step.

Textbook recommendation. If the number of candidates is not too large, use all possible regressions with the minimum $MS_E$ and $C_p$ criteria: it finds the best equation for those criteria, which stepwise methods do not guarantee, and it is not distorted by dependencies among regressors. $C_p$ uses $MS_E$ of the full model as the estimate of $\sigma^2$; a model with negligible bias has $C_p\approx p$, and one chooses the minimum $C_p$ or a model with a slightly larger $C_p$ that is not much biased. A final model should always be checked with residuals, lack of fit and influence, and several methods should be compared since no single “best” equation need exist.

Selecting a model with the same data used to test it makes the reported $t$ and $F$ statistics and $P$-values too optimistic, because the winner of many comparisons was chosen because it looked good. Validate the final model on fresh data or by cross-validation (Chapter 14), and prefer subject-matter judgement to blind automation.
Multicollinearity
Multicollinearity means that some regressors are nearly linear combinations of others, so $X\T X$ is nearly singular. The variance inflation factor of $x_j$ is
\mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac1{1-R_j^2},
where $R_j^2$ is the $R^2$ from regressing $x_j$ on the remaining regressors.

One can show $\Var[\hat\beta_j]=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{jj}}\mathrm{VIF}_j$ (with $S_{jj}=\sum(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_j)^2$), so VIF is the factor by which collinearity inflates the variance. The textbook rule: $\mathrm{VIF}_j>10$ ($R_j^2>0.9$) signals a problem, though some authors consider $10$ too liberal and use $4$ or $5$ as the limit. Symptoms: large standard errors and unstable coefficients (signs that flip with small changes in the data), a significant overall $F$ with no significant individual $t$’s, and an $X\T X$ with a very small eigenvalue (condition number $\kappa(X\T X)=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}>1000$). Remedies: remove or combine redundant regressors, collect data that spread the regressors, centre variables, or use ridge regression or principal components regression. Predictions within the range of the data can still be fine; it is the interpretation of individual coefficients that suffers.

Remedies listed in the textbook: augment the data with new observations designed to break the near-dependencies (often impossible for cost or physical reasons); delete regressors (at the price of discarding their information); or use an estimator less sensitive to collinearity, such as ridge regression. Even with collinearity the fitted equation can still predict well by interpolation inside the original region of $x$-space, since $\mathbf{x}\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ may be well estimated though individual $\hat\beta_j$ are not; extrapolation needs good individual estimates and generally fails.
Ridge Regression (CD Only)

For $\lambda\ge0$, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_R=(X\T X+\lambda I)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$ (with the regressors standardised and the intercept left unpenalised). It minimises $SS_E+\lambda\sum_{j\ge1}\beta_j^2$.

In practice $\lambda$ is chosen by solving for several values (on standardised data, usually $0<\lambda<1$) and inspecting a plot of the coefficients against $\lambda$, the ridge trace: take $\lambda$ as small as possible that still stabilises the estimates, because variance decreases and squared bias increases with $\lambda$. The ridge estimator is biased but has smaller variance, and for a suitable $\lambda>0$ a smaller mean square error than least squares when collinearity is severe. It shrinks the coefficients toward zero, most strongly along directions in which the data carry little information (the small singular values of $X$; see Linear Algebra, Chapter 17). The value of $\lambda$ is chosen by cross-validation or from the ridge trace (plot of the coefficients against $\lambda$).
Nonlinear Regression Models (CD Only)

Some models are intrinsically nonlinear in the parameters, for example $Y=\theta_1\big(1-e^{-\theta_2x}\big)+\varepsilon$. The least squares estimates minimise $\sum\big(y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\big)^2$ but there is no closed-form solution; one iterates, for example by the Gauss–Newton method: linearise $f$ about the current estimate, $f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)\approx f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta^{(m)})+J_i(\boldsymbol\theta-\boldsymbol\theta^{(m)})$, solve the resulting linear least squares problem for the step, and repeat until convergence. Good starting values (often from a transformation or from physical insight) are important, and the usual $t$ and $F$ tests hold only approximately (for large $n$).

Model $\mathbf{y}=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon$; $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\mathbf{y}$; $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=H\mathbf{y}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\Col X$; $\hat\sigma^2=SS_E/(n-p)$, $p=k+1$.
$\Cov[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}]=\sigma^2(X\T X)^{-1}$; $\se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2C_{jj}}$; Gauss–Markov; normal errors give $t$ and $\chi^2$ distributions.

Overall test $F_0=MS_R/MS_E\sim F_{k,n-p}$; individual tests $t_0=\hat\beta_j/\se(\hat\beta_j)\sim t_{n-p}$; subsets by partial $F$ with the extra sum of squares; $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$ for comparing models.
Mean response $\mathbf{x}_0\T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\pm t\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2\mathbf{x}_0\T(X\T X)^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0}$; prediction adds $1$ under the root.
Diagnostics: studentised residuals, leverage $h_{ii}>2p/n$, Cook’s $D_i>1$, PRESS; check for hidden extrapolation.

Modeling: polynomial terms (centre them), indicator variables ($m-1$ for $m$ levels), selection by $C_p$/AIC/stepwise (beware optimism), multicollinearity via $\mathrm{VIF}>10$, ridge as a remedy, Gauss–Newton for nonlinear models.

For the running example, construct the analysis of variance table, test $H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=0$ at $\alpha=0.05$ and compute $R^2$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$. Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\beta_2$.
For the running example, find the $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean response and the $95\%$ prediction interval at $(x_1,x_2)=(-1,1)$ and at $(0,0)$. Why is the second interval narrower?
Show that $H=X(X\T X)^{-1}X\T$ is symmetric and idempotent, that $\tr H=p$, and that $0\le h_{ii}\le1$. Show also that $(I-H)X=0$.

A regression with $n=25$ and $k=4$ regressors gives $SS_R=420$ and $SS_E=180$. Test the significance of regression, compute $R^2$ and $R^2_{\mathrm{adj}}$. Adding two more regressors raises $SS_R$ to $438$; test whether the two added regressors are jointly significant.
Regressing $x_3$ on $x_1,x_2$ gives $R_3^2=0.96$. Find $\mathrm{VIF}_3$ and explain what it implies for the standard error of $\hat\beta_3$ relative to uncorrelated regressors.

Write the design matrix for a model with one quantitative regressor $x$ and a three-level factor (levels A, B, C) with indicator variables, for the six observations $(x,\text{level})$: $(1,A),(2,A),(3,B),(4,B),(5,C),(6,C)$. Interpret each coefficient.
In a regression with $n=20$, $p=3$ one observation has $h_{ii}=0.62$ and studentised residual $r_i=2.1$. Compute Cook’s distance and decide whether it is influential; compare $h_{ii}$ with $2p/n$.

Show that for ridge regression with $X\T X=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_p)$ each coefficient is the least squares coefficient multiplied by $\lambda_j/(\lambda_j+\lambda)$, and describe what this does to coefficients whose regressors carry little information.
